title: The Sharpe Pint: Palantir's Print, the Hormuz Relief Valve, and Why Short-Term Trend Broke

opening_mood.text: Morning. If you spent the last few weeks of summer clutching your stomach and staring at red screens, you can finally put the antacids away. The City has found its mojo again, fueled by a sudden outbreak of diplomatic optimism in the Middle East and a blockbuster print from Palantir that has, for now, silenced the AI doomers. Grab a coffee—or a pint, depending on how your book is looking—and let's get into it.

content.text: Palantir's 'Otherworldly' Print Defies the AI Skeptics

Palantir (PLTR) dropped a Q2 earnings bomb that has temporarily silenced the AI ROI doomers. Overall revenue surged 93% year-over-year to $1.935 billion, comfortably beating Wall Street's $1.8 billion estimate. The real kicker? US commercial revenue skyrocketed 149% to $764 million, while its Rule of 40 score (growth rate + profit margin) hit a mind-boggling 155%. The stock jumped over 12% after-hours, pushing its valuation toward the $350 billion mark.

Why it matters: While the rest of Big Tech is facing 'AI jitters' as investors demand to know when the trillions in capex will actually show up on the bottom line, Alex Karp's outfit is proving they can turn tokens into actual economic value. Palantir's Artificial Intelligence Platform (AIP) is scaling at pace, and their 'AI sovereignty' pitch—promising enterprises that their data won't be used to train competitors' models—is landing beautifully.

The City Angle: The valuation is, frankly, in fantasyland territory. Even with upgraded guidance (full-year revenue raised to $8.15 billion), PLTR is trading at over 40x forward sales and roughly 75x free cash flow. It's a classic battle between spectacular operational execution and a multiple that assumes they will eventually run the entire global economy.

Over a pint: "Karp’s print is the ultimate antidote to the AI bubble narrative. 149% US commercial growth is staggering. But at 40x forward sales, you're pricing in flawless execution until the end of the decade. Is it a generational software monopoly, or just the most expensive momentum trade on the board?"
AMD: AI Data Centers Boom, but the Consumer is Slacking

AMD reported Q2 2026 revenue of $11.5 billion, up 50% year-over-year, beating the $11.28 billion consensus. The star of the show was the Data Center division, where revenue more than doubled YoY to represent 58% of the business. CEO Lisa Su teased accelerating demand for EPYC CPUs and the scaling of their Instinct GPU deployments, with next-gen Helios chips ramping up. However, gaming revenue plunged 31% due to sluggish consumer demand.

Why it matters: It’s a tale of two tech sectors. Enterprise demand for AI compute is insatiable, but the everyday consumer is keeping their wallet firmly shut when it comes to upgrading consoles and PCs. Despite the top-and-bottom-line beat and strong Q3 guidance ($13 billion vs. $12.5 billion expected), the stock wobbled slightly post-earnings as investors fretted over flat gross margins.

The City Angle: AMD is successfully positioning itself as the only viable alternative to Nvidia's data center hegemony. But challenging the king isn't cheap. AMD is having to spend heavily on capex and supply chain commitments to secure advanced packaging capacity, which is keeping a lid on short-term margin expansion.

Over a pint: "AMD's data center business doubling shows the AI hardware buildout isn't slowing down. But that 31% drop in gaming is a reminder that the consumer side of tech is still in the doldrums. Lisa Su is doing a brilliant job, but scaling up to fight Nvidia is a capital-intensive slog."
Ferguson Joins the S&P 500: The Final Nail in its FTSE Coffin

Plumbing and HVAC distributor Ferguson Enterprises (FERG) officially joined the S&P 500 index on August 5, replacing video-game publisher Electronic Arts (which is being taken private). The inclusion marks the final step in Ferguson's five-year migration from a London-listed FTSE 100 stalwart (formerly known as Wolseley) to a solely NYSE-listed, US-headquartered giant.

Why it matters: The stock jumped over 8% on the announcement. Why? Because joining the S&P 500 plugs Ferguson directly into the massive plumbing of passive investing—forcing thousands of index funds and ETFs benchmarked to the index to buy its shares.

The City Angle: This is another painful, high-profile black eye for the London Stock Exchange. Ferguson's migration is the ultimate validation of the 'listing arbitrage' trade. By moving to New York, they secured a higher valuation, deeper liquidity, and now, a coveted spot in the world's premier equity index.

Over a pint: "When a plumbing distributor gets an 8% pop just on index inclusion, you can see why London boards are looking across the Atlantic with envy. Ferguson's S&P 500 entry is the ultimate proof that leaving the FTSE for the NYSE was the right commercial move, even if it hurts our pride in the City."
Polymarket's Wildfire Bets Spark Senate Backlash

A group of Democratic US senators has urged the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) to crack down on prediction markets allowing bets on natural disasters, specifically wildfires. The lawmakers expressed deep concern that allowing people to wager on the destruction of acreage—such as the $1.2 million traded on Polymarket over California blazes—creates a perverse incentive for arson.

Why it matters: Prediction markets have exploded in popularity over the past 18 months, transitioning from niche crypto playgrounds to mainstream macro indicators. However, they are hitting a major regulatory and ethical wall. While Polymarket argues that these contracts provide invaluable, real-time, market-based risk pricing, politicians see a moral hazard.

The City Angle: For quants and macro traders, prediction markets are increasingly treated as high-fidelity alternative data. If regulators start banning contracts based on 'public interest' or moral hazard, it threatens to neuter the utility of these platforms as genuine hedging and forecasting tools.

Over a pint: "The Senate's push against wildfire betting highlights the ethical frontier of prediction markets. While traders love the pure, real-time data, the moral hazard of letting someone short-squeeze a forest fire is a tough sell to the public. It’s the classic clash between market efficiency and basic human decency."
The Death of Globalization: Trade Interventions Hit All-Time High

New data from the WTO and IMF reveals that global trade policy interventions have reached an all-time high in early 2026. The Trade Policy Activity Index shows that protectionist measures—primarily restrictive tariffs, import bans, and massive state subsidies—ran at nearly double 2024 levels from January to May, marking the highest peak since the 2008 financial crisis.

Why it matters: The post-Cold War era of hyper-globalization is officially dead. We have entered a structural 'subsidy arms race' as the US, EU, and China aggressively use state aid to ring-fence critical supply chains, particularly in semiconductors, green energy, and critical minerals.

The City Angle: For asset managers, the 'low-inflation, high-efficiency' supply chain model of the last 30 years is gone. Companies will face structurally higher input costs. Picking winners now requires analyzing geopolitical alignment and a firm's ability to capture state subsidies, rather than just pure operational efficiency.

Over a pint: "The WTO/IMF data is the statistical proof of what we've all suspected: globalization is in reverse. For stock pickers, the game has changed. It's no longer about who has the cheapest factory in Asia, but who is best at lobbying for state handouts and dodging tariffs."

sections.title: Markets Briefing: What Moved and Why

content.text: The Bulls Reclaim the City

If you spent the summer sweating over a correction, you can officially put the antacids away. Wall Street didn't just bounce on Tuesday; it staged a full-blown, broad-based melt-up that sent records tumbling. The Dow Jones surged 907 points (1.71%) to breach the 54,000 milestone for the first time, closing at 54,085.88. The S&P 500 jumped 1.79% to 7,737, securing its first record close since June and fully erasing its summer losses. Meanwhile, the tech-heavy Nasdaq led the charge, leaping 2.58% to 26,585. Overnight, the party travelled east, with Japan's Nikkei 225 jumping 3.2% to 66,002.
The 'Hormuz Ceasefire' Trade

The primary fuel for this cross-asset rally was a sudden, dramatic outbreak of diplomatic optimism. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent went on CNBC to announce that the US, Iran, and Oman are on the cusp of an interim deal to reopen the blockaded Strait of Hormuz, potentially as early as Wednesday (5 August). President Trump added his usual flair, calling it Iran's 'last chance before decapitation' but confirming that talks are 'going on right now.'

For markets, this was the ultimate relief valve. The Strait of Hormuz is the transit point for a fifth of the world's oil and LNG. Stripping out that geopolitical risk premium sent WTI crude tumbling down to around $76 a barrel, while Brent crude fell over 5% to around $78.43. Cheaper energy means lower inflation risk, which in turn gave bonds a lift, dragging the 10-year US Treasury yield down to 4.63%.
Palantir's 'Otherworldly' Cash and SpaceX's Capital Burn

On the corporate front, the AI trade proved it actually has teeth when it comes to generating cold, hard cash. Palantir (PLTR) surged a staggering 29.5% after reporting what CEO Alex Karp called an 'otherworldly' Q2. US commercial revenue skyrocketed 149% year-over-year, silencing the sceptics who thought AI was all expensive GPUs and no actual invoices.

Meanwhile, Elon Musk's SpaceX (SPCX)—which pulled off a historic IPO in June—reported its first-ever quarterly earnings as a public company. The numbers were a classic Musk mixed bag: Q2 revenue beat expectations at $7.8 billion (vs $6.8 billion expected), but the company logged a $541 million net loss. The culprit? A massive CapEx bill of $15.8 billion as they pour cash into Starlink and orbiting AI data centres. While the stock gained 9% in the regular session, it slid 5% after-hours. The market is increasingly intolerant of endless capital burn, and traders are also eyeing a massive insider share lock-up expiration on 6 August.
Under the Hood: The VIX Paradox

If everything is so rosy, why is the VIX ticking up? In an unusual cross-asset quirk, the VIX actually edged higher to 16.50 alongside the stock market rally. Normally, when equities go up, volatility goes down. This divergence tells us that institutional desks aren't entirely buying the euphoria. They are actively buying downside protection (hedging) ahead of Friday's US employment report. It's a classic 'risk-on, but keep one eye on the exit' setup.

content.text: The Magic Metric of Credit: Duration Times Spread (DTS)

If you’ve ever sat through a fixed-income presentation, you’ve probably heard people drone on about spread duration. It’s the standard textbook way to measure how much a bond’s price will move if its credit spread changes. But there’s a massive, real-world flaw in how most beginners think about it: they assume that when the market gets hit, all credit spreads widen by the same absolute amount. In the real world, credit markets don't move in parallel lines; they move in percentages. Enter Duration Times Spread (DTS)—the industry-standard metric that actually reflects how credit risk behaves when the world is ending.
The Core Concept: Spreads Move in Percentages, Not Basis Points

Imagine two bonds. Bond A is a rock-solid, investment-grade corporate bond trading at a credit spread of 50 basis points (bps) over risk-free rates. Bond B is a spicy high-yield bond trading at a spread of 500 bps. If a market shock hits, Bond A’s spread isn't going to widen by 100 bps to 150 bps while Bond B’s widens by 100 bps to 600 bps. That’s not how credit works. Instead, spreads tend to move proportionally. If spreads widen by 10% across the board, Bond A’s spread widens by 5 bps (to 55 bps), while Bond B’s widens by 50 bps (to 550 bps).

Because credit volatility is proportional to the spread level, you can’t measure credit risk by spread duration alone. You have to multiply the two. Originally developed by researchers at Robeco in 2003 and published with Lehman Brothers in 2007, DTS is calculated as:
DTS = Spread Duration x Option-Adjusted Spread (OAS)

By multiplying the bond's sensitivity to spread changes (spread duration) by its actual spread (which acts as a proxy for its riskiness and volatility), you get a single, beautiful number that represents the bond's true credit volatility.
A Quick Pub-Maths Example
Let’s compare two bonds in a portfolio:

items: Bond A (Long-dated Investment Grade): Spread Duration of 8.0 years, trading at an OAS of 80 bps. DTS = 8.0 x 80 = 640.
Bond B (Short-dated High Yield): Spread Duration of 2.0 years, trading at an OAS of 400 bps. DTS = 2.0 x 400 = 800.

content.text: If you only looked at spread duration, you’d think Bond A is four times riskier than Bond B. But because Bond B has a much wider spread, its DTS is actually higher (800 vs 640). If the credit market experiences a systematic 10% widening:

items: Bond A’s spread widens by 8 bps (10% of 80). Price drop = 8 bps x 8.0 years = 0.64%.
Bond B’s spread widens by 40 bps (10% of 400). Price drop = 40 bps x 2.0 years = 0.80%.

content.text: The actual price drop is exactly proportional to their DTS. Bond B, despite its short maturity, is the riskier position. DTS caught this; traditional spread duration missed it completely.
Why This Matters in Asset Management

If you are managing a credit portfolio, matching your benchmark’s spread duration is not enough. If you match spread duration but buy wider-spread bonds (underweighting tight-spread bonds), you are running a massive, unhedged bet on credit volatility. In the institutional world (using systems like Bloomberg PORT or MSCI RiskMetrics), portfolio managers track Active DTS to ensure they aren't taking accidental credit bets. It also allows managers to compare risk across completely different asset classes—like comparing a 10-year single-A corporate bond to a 2-year double-B high-yield bond.
The Common Beginner Mistake

The classic mistake is confusing modified duration (which measures sensitivity to risk-free interest rates) with spread duration (which measures sensitivity to credit spreads), and then ignoring the spread level itself. A bond can have a very low interest rate duration (e.g., because it’s floating-rate or short-dated) but still carry massive credit risk. If you only look at duration, you’ll walk right into a high-yield buzzsaw when spreads widen.
How to Use This in Interviews and at Work

If you’re interviewing for a credit research, fixed income, or quant portfolio management role, dropping DTS into the conversation is an instant credibility booster. It shows you understand how institutional portfolios are actually constructed, rather than just reciting textbook formulas.

If you want to sound like you actually know credit, don't just talk about duration. Ask how they manage their risk budget. A great question to ask a credit PM is: 'When you're constructing your portfolios, do you manage credit risk using active spread duration, or do you strictly target active DTS to account for the proportional volatility of wider-spread names?'

Over a pint with colleagues, you can use it to critique a trade: 'Sure, that short-duration high-yield paper looks like a safe way to pick up carry, but have you looked at the DTS contribution? We’re taking on way more credit volatility than the duration suggests.'

sections.title: Quant / AI Finance Idea of the Day

content.text: The Latent Risk Whisperer: Deep Regime Mixtures (DeRegiME)

If you've ever deployed a deep learning model to forecast asset returns, you've likely run into the painful reality of the mean-variance mismatch. Your model might get the direction right, but when the market regime shifts from a quiet summer lull to a full-blown liquidity crisis, your static risk bounds get absolutely shredded. Traditional neural forecasters are great at predicting the conditional mean, but they are notoriously bad at handling distribution shifts in the residuals—the variance, covariance, and tail thickness of the noise.

Enter DeRegiME (Deep Regime Mixture of Experts), a framework developed by researchers at the Oxford-Man Institute of Quantitative Finance. Instead of treating uncertainty as a single, static distribution or an uninterpretable black-box mixture, DeRegiME explicitly separates the underlying signal from latent uncertainty regimes. It softly assigns each forecast to a set of learned, recurring regimes using a sparse variational Gaussian Process (GP) with a Student-t likelihood.
How It Works

Rather than running multiple separate models (which is computationally ruinous and prone to overfitting), DeRegiME uses a single backbone network (like PatchTST) to predict the mean, and a shared "gate" to dynamically assign the current market state to a sparse set of regimes:

items: The Mean: A standard deep learning backbone handles the conditional mean of the time series.
The Gate: A stick-breaking gating network outputs soft probabilities for which regime the market is currently in, automatically pruning unused regimes to keep the model sparse and interpretable.
The Residuals: A sparse variational Gaussian Process models the regime-dependent covariance.
The Tails: A Student-t likelihood head adjusts its scale and degrees of freedom (fatness of the tails) based on the active regime.

content.text: A Quick Python Look
Here is a simplified conceptual look at how you might implement a gating mechanism to mix regime-specific uncertainty parameters (scale and degrees of freedom) for a Student-t distribution:

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class SimpleRegimeGate(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_dim, num_regimes):
        super().__init__()
        self.gate = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(input_dim, 32),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(32, num_regimes),
            nn.Softmax(dim=-1)
        )
        self.regime_scales = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(num_regimes))
        self.regime_dfs = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(num_regimes) * 5.0)

    def forward(self, x, predicted_mean):
        regime_weights = self.gate(x)
        mixed_scale = torch.sum(regime_weights * torch.exp(self.regime_scales), dim=-1)
        mixed_df = torch.sum(regime_weights * torch.clamp(self.regime_dfs, min=2.1), dim=-1)
        return predicted_mean, mixed_scale, mixed_df
Why This Matters in the City

In a macro hedge fund or an asset management shop, you don't just care about the point forecast; you care about the distribution. If you are running a trend-following strategy, knowing whether you are in a high-volatility, fat-tailed regime versus a low-volatility, mean-reverting regime dictates your position sizing and stop-loss placement. DeRegiME's beauty is that it doesn't just output a wider confidence interval; it actually identifies the implicit changepoints where the market transitioned from one regime to another, giving you a clear, interpretable diagnostic of market stress.
The Interview / Pub Conversation Angle
If you're chatting with a portfolio manager or interviewing for a quant role, this is a brilliant way to show you understand the limits of standard ML. You can frame it like this:

Most deep learning models fail in production because they assume the residual noise is stationary. In reality, the mean expected return might look identical on two different days, but the tail risk is completely different. By using a Deep Regime Mixture like DeRegiME, we can jointly model the mean signal and softly assign the residuals to latent uncertainty regimes using a gated variational Gaussian Process. This gives us dynamically scaling risk bounds and explicit regime interpretability without the computational overhead of running multiple independent models.

sections.title: One Article or Paper Worth Reading

content.text: If you have spent any time around systematic macro or CTA desks over the last decade, you will have heard the same collective sigh: "Short-term trend is dead." For over two centuries, buying what was going up and selling what was going down was the closest thing to a free lunch in finance. Then, around 2009, the fast-trend machine just broke. A brand-new paper from the quant royalty at Capital Fund Management (CFM)—including the legendary Jean-Philippe Bouchaud—finally gives us a brilliant, microstructural explanation of why.

items: Title: Is Trend Still Your Friend?: A Microstructural Account of the Demise of Short-Term Trend-Following (arXiv:2607.01550, July 2026).
Authors: Jutta G. Kurth, Zoltan Eisler, Adam Rej, and Jean-Philippe Bouchaud.
The core puzzle: Why did an anomaly that survived two world wars, the Great Depression, and the dot-com crash suddenly fall off a cliff post-GFC?

content.text: The Usual Suspects (And Why They Are Wrong)

Before delivering their own verdict, the authors systematically dismantle the excuses CTAs have been giving disgruntled clients for fifteen years. It is not "capacity constraints" (CTA assets have actually stagnated since 2010 while the decay got worse). It is not just "electronification" or "crowding" either. Instead, the authors split the futures market into two camps using a metric most macro allocators completely ignore: volatility-normalised tick size.
The Small-Tick vs. Large-Tick Divide

The paper's big empirical reveal is that trend following has not died everywhere. It has died specifically on small-tick contracts (like equity index futures and major FX pairs), where the minimum price increment is tiny relative to daily volatility. On these contracts, trend PnL has completely collapsed. Meanwhile, on large-tick contracts (like short-term interest rates, bonds, and certain commodities), where the tick size is structurally fat, trend following is still alive and kicking.
The Self-Fulfilling Loop is Broken

Why does tick size matter so much? The authors argue that trend following has always been a self-fulfilling prophecy. A trend signal triggers directional buying, which has market impact, pushing the price up, which reinforces the trend signal and brings in more buyers. It is a beautiful, momentum-generating feedback loop.

Enter the High-Frequency Traders (HFTs) post-2008. On small-tick contracts, order books are "dense" and spreads are tight. HFT market makers can easily spot predictable, slow-moving CTA order flow and withdraw liquidity or adjust quotes ahead of it. This severs the feedback loop. Without the market impact of the trend followers actually driving the price, the trend signal decays and the alpha vanishes. On large-tick contracts, the order books are structurally "sparse" (because stepping in front of a large tick is expensive and risky), so HFTs cannot play the same game. The loop holds.

Both the profitability and the persistence of trend are sustained by this impact channel... the post-crisis transition to HFT-dominated market making [has] sharply contrasting consequences for sparse (small-tick) and dense [market structures].
The Kicker: Even with Zero Fees, You Lose

The most alarming finding for systematic traders is that even if you backtest small-tick trend strategies with zero transaction costs, they still flatline. This is not a case of execution costs eating your lunch. The lunch itself has been thrown in the bin. The underlying price action has changed because the microstructural feedback loop has been broken.
What to Skim vs. What to Read

items: Read: Sections 5 and 6. This is where they explain the tick-size split and lay out the self-fulfilling loop mechanism. It is pure market microstructure gold.
Skim: Section 4 (the debunking of capacity and electronification) and the appendices, unless you really want to see the volume-clock decompositions.

content.text: How to Use This at Work (or in an Interview)

items: In an interview: If you are interviewing at a quant fund, CTA, or multi-strat, and they ask you about trend-following or momentum, do not just say "it is crowded." Drop this paper. Explain that the demise of short-term trend is a microstructural story about volatility-normalised tick sizes and the breaking of the self-fulfilling price impact loop by HFTs. It shows you actually understand how markets clear, rather than just reading retail trading blogs.

With colleagues: Use it to challenge the asset allocation team. If they are allocating to CTAs or systematic macro, are they adjusting their trend models for tick-size regimes? A generic trend-following model that treats the S&P 500 mini and Eurodollar/Short Sterling futures the same way is fundamentally flawed.

content.text: The Sharpe Pint Take

This is easily one of the best quant papers of the year. It bridges the gap between high-level asset management (macro trends) and low-level market microstructure (HFT order books). It also serves as a stark warning: market anomalies are not just passive patterns waiting to be harvested; they are often dynamic feedback loops. When the plumbing of the market changes, the macro anomalies we take for granted can simply evaporate.

content.text: The Von Restorff Effect (The "Red Apple" Principle)

Picture the scene: you are sitting in an investment committee meeting. The presenting team is on slide 27 of a 45-slide deck. Every single slide so far has featured the exact same layout: a dark blue header, three bullet points in Arial 11pt, and a complex bar chart that requires squinting to read. Your brain, in its infinite wisdom, has decided to enter low-power standby mode. You are physically present, but mentally you are deciding what to have for dinner.
Then, slide 28 appears. It has no bullet points. It has no bar chart. It is a solid black slide with a single, massive, bright yellow number in the middle: -42%.

Suddenly, your brain snaps back online. You sit up. When the meeting ends, you might not remember the EBITDA projections from slide 12 or the synergy estimates from slide 22, but you will absolutely remember that -42%.

This is the Von Restorff Effect (also known as the Isolation Effect). Coined by German psychiatrist Hedwig von Restorff in 1933, the principle is simple: when multiple similar items are presented, the one that differs from the rest is the one that gets remembered. Our brains are highly efficient pattern-recognition machines. When a pattern is predictable, we stop paying close attention to conserve energy. But when an element breaks the pattern, the brain pauses, attention sharpens, and memory encoding goes into overdrive.
Why it matters in the City

In finance, we are constantly competing for the scarcest commodity in the square mile: attention. Whether you are pitching a deal to a client, trying to get a buy-side analyst to read your research note, or applying for a new job, you are usually operating in a sea of extreme sameness.

items: The CV Trap: If you are an analyst or associate applying for a role, your CV probably looks identical to 200 others. You all have "strong financial modeling skills," you all "assisted on cross-border M&A transactions," and you all "graduated with honours." To an interviewer reading their 40th CV of the day, you are a blur of corporate beige. But if you have one highly distinct, unusual, yet impressive detail—like "Built an open-source Python library used by 500 quants" or "Completed a 100km ultra-marathon"—you break the pattern. You cease to be "Analyst #14" and become "the ultra-marathon analyst."

The Pitch Deck "Visual Speed Bump": Most pitch decks are designed to be uniform to maintain "brand consistency." While a clean aesthetic is good, absolute uniformity is a cognitive sedative. If you want the client to remember your fee structure or your unique edge, you need to isolate it. Make that slide look completely different from the rest of the deck.

Client Emails: If you send a weekly market update that looks like a wall of text, it will be deleted. If you isolate one key "Insight of the Week" at the top in a bold, highlighted box, that is the only part they will read—and the only part they will remember.

content.text: How to use it this week

You don't need to start wearing a neon suit to the office to stand out. In fact, the Von Restorff effect only works if the background is highly consistent. If everything is loud, nothing is. Here is how to apply it subtly and strategically:

items: Design "Visual Speed Bumps": In your next presentation, identify the single most important slide—the one you want the committee to discuss over lunch. Change its background color to a contrasting tone, or strip out all the text and use a single, powerful visual.

The "One-Thing" Email: When emailing a senior stakeholder with a list of updates, don't make them guess what matters. Bold the single most critical action item, or put it in a separate, single-sentence paragraph.

Find Your "Red Apple": Look at your CV or your LinkedIn bio. If you stripped away your job title and company name, is there a single line that couldn't be written by any of your peers? If not, find a genuine, distinctive achievement or interest and put it front and center.

content.text: If you make everything bold, nothing is bold. If you isolate one thing, it becomes unforgettable.
One line to remember
In a sea of corporate navy, be the single red tie.

The Dow crossed 54,000 for the first time as hopes of a US-Iran-Oman deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz sent oil tumbling.
Ferguson's entry into the S&P 500 marks the final step of its migration from London, delivering another blow to the LSE.
